sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on the centred masthead "The Wexley Gazette", drops past the double rule, and runs left to right across three equal story headlines. It reads as the front page of a small local paper, quiet and traditional. The bottom ~45% of the frame (y≈420–800) is empty. Assumed job: give local readers three short news items they can scan quickly.

The whole piece:
- One-sentence purpose: yes
- Image and headline as one idea: yes (there is no image, so the line does not apply)
- Every element does a job: yes (the double rule is the usual newspaper masthead device and separates the paper's name from the news)
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished, no placeholder or typos: yes
- Repeated elements look the same: yes
- Mood fits the message: yes
- Headings name their sections: yes

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The page reads as one thing.** The bold serif masthead, the double rule, the serif body text and plain black on white all belong to the same traditional printed-newspaper tradition, so a first-time viewer knows within a second that this is a local paper. Keep the type family and the rule together. Swapping in a sans or adding colour accents would break that.
- **The headlines are real headlines.** "Bridge to reopen in spring", "Market moves indoors" and "School wins garden prize" each name who does what, with a verb. A reader can scan the three across the top (y≈155) and get the news without reading a single body line. The body copy is finished, specific and consistent, for example cars in April and people on foot from March.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. The masthead "The Wexley Gazette" (centred, about x 478–802, y 35–72) gets the first look, but only barely: it looks about 1.4× the headline size and has the same weight and colour. After it come three stories that are the same in every way: same bold headline at about 24 px (y≈155), same justified body at the same size, same 330 px column at x 100, 470 and 840. None of them leads. The reader gets the paper's name and then three equal choices, so they read left to right by habit and the page never says what today's main news is. A newspaper front page exists to rank the news, and this page doesn't. The empty bottom half (y≈420–800) makes it worse: the space is there for a lead story to be much bigger, but it's left unused. This is Tschichold's point (*The New Typography*) that size differences should show the order of importance, and Hofmann's on contrast of scale (*Graphic Design Manual*): when every main element is the same size, the page has no tension. Fix: pick the lead story, probably the bridge reopening since it affects the most readers, and make it clearly the first thing seen. Give it a much larger headline and a wider measure, for example two columns, or the full width above the other two. Set the other two back as secondary stories. Kept as it is, the masthead is the only anchor, and it is too close in size to the headlines to anchor firmly. Defect (it hides the order of the news, which is the page's job), supported by convention. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- There are three clearly separate text levels: masthead about 34 px bold, headlines about 24 px bold, body about 18 px regular. No two sizes are close enough to be confused, so masthead, headline and story are each obvious at a glance.
- Headlines differ from body text by weight as well as size (bold serif against regular serif), so each story's start is easy to pick out without needing colour.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (one element stands clearly above the rest)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** All the content sits in the top half. The masthead, rule and three stories end by about y 415, and from y 415 to the bottom at about y 800 the page is empty across its full width. The page looks like it was cut off or failed to load more stories, and everything feels pushed up against the masthead. The three columns also end at different heights: the left and middle columns at about y 404, the right at about y 378. With nothing below them, those ragged ends become the edge of the whole layout. All the weight is on top and nothing below holds it down (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). If this is the whole page, the fix is to fill the frame:
   - add more content below, such as a second row of stories, a lead picture, or a footer or dateline band;
   - or, if three stories are all there is, size the canvas to the content.

   If this is a capture of a longer page that is still loading, the gap is fine. A fixed-height screenshot showing only this is not. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** The double rule under the masthead spans x 100–1180, but the columns span x 100–1170: three 330 px columns with 40 px gutters. So the right edge of the justified right column stops about 10 px short of where the rule ends. The left edges line up, the right edges nearly do, and the eye reads the near-miss as an error. A placement that is neither clearly aligned nor clearly off makes the whole look unfinished (Arnheim, ch. I). Make the rule and the text block share one right edge: either end the rule at 1170 or widen the columns to fill 1080 px. Defect (a small one). Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **The column grid.** Three equal 330 px columns with one 40 px gutter, all hanging from the same top line, give a calm, steady rhythm that reads as a newspaper at once.
- **Baselines across columns.** Body lines in all three columns sit on the same baselines (y ≈ 196, 222, 248…), and so do the three headings. Reading across the page feels orderly even though every column is justified.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty lower half is the end of the page or a capture taken before more content loaded. Check the live page or the source file.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (elements exactly aligned or clearly off; visual weight balances)

sections.report:
The walk and the source entries are done, and I'm writing the report now.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Does justified text keep even word spaces, with no holes or rivers of white?"** and **"Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?"** These are one problem with one cause.
   - **Where:** all three columns are fully justified at about 330 px wide, which comes to about 34–42 characters a line. "Engineers found that two of the five" is 36. That is short of the 45–75 range, and also a bit under Bringhurst's 40–50 for text set in several columns.
   - **What the viewer meets:** squeezing so few words into each line opens clear holes between words:
     - column 1, "months of repairs to its arches." (y≈247)
     - column 2, "the old corn exchange from next" (y≈221), "month, ending forty years in the" (y≈247) and "a stage for local bands on the first" (y≈377)
     - column 3, "a regional prize for the vegetable" (y≈221) and "feeds the school kitchen two days a" (y≈299)
   - **Why it matters:** the grey of each column turns blotchy, and the stretched lines read in jerks. This is the most visible flaw on an otherwise clean page.
   - **Source:** Hochuli, *Detail in Typography*, p. 34: under about 50 characters, "even wordspacing becomes difficult, if not impossible". Bringhurst, §2.1.1–2.1.2: short justified lines give "white acne".
   - **Fix:** set the columns ragged right, or turn on hyphenation if you keep them justified. The page has a lot of empty space, so widening the measure toward 45+ characters (for example two columns, or a smaller gutter) would also help.
   - **Type:** defect for the word spacing, convention for the measure. **Weight:** minor. The text is still readable; it is a matter of texture and polish.

**What's working.**
- **Type plan:** one serif family is used throughout, with bold for the masthead and headlines and regular for body. That gives a clear three-level scale with no near-miss sizes. Keep it.
- **Body text:** it is a generous size (about 18 px) in near-black on white, with comfortable leading. It reads easily, and every headline sits on a single line with no awkward breaks.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; justified text keeps even word spaces)

Walk notes (Color). First read: the eye goes to the masthead "The Wexley Gazette", then to the three bold headlines. It's a plain, quiet local news front page in near-black serif type on white. Assumption: it's a web front page for a small-town paper, read by local residents.

- Small palette: yes. Only near-black ink (about #222, slightly cool) on white, with no hue.
- Strong colour kept to a small area: yes. There is no saturated colour.
- Clear light/dark range that holds in grayscale: yes. It's dark ink on white, and the structure comes from weight and size.
- Warm colours forward, cool ones back: yes. There's no hue, so nothing breaks this.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. Headlines, body text and rules all use the same ink.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. No colour carries meaning.
- Dark theme uses dark gray, not black: yes. The page is light.

None of the lines is no or unsure, so I skipped step 5.

**Section.** Color: applies. It's a page with only neutral colours, so every line can still be judged.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- There's one dark, slightly cool near-black (not pure #000) on white, used for the masthead, headlines, body text and the double rule. Value alone carries the structure, so the page reads the same in grayscale or in print, and the reader has no stray colour to sort out. Keep the single ink colour if colour is added later.
- With no accent colour, the bold weight and larger size of the masthead and headlines are what create the hierarchy, and that is enough here. This suits a quiet, newsprint-style local paper. If an accent is ever added, for a section label or a link, it should be one hue on a small share of the page.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon or other picture. It is a text-only newspaper page: a masthead, a double rule, and three columns of headlines and body text.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image is a three-column newspaper page with a masthead and three short text stories. It has no chart, no table of figures, no dashboard and no headline metric. The figures in the text ("eighteen months", "sixty stalls", "forty years") are written out in prose, not shown as data.

**Findings**
None.
